title: Rotation and torque
note: Rotation mirrors straight-line motion: angle for position, ω for velocity, α for acceleration, torque for force, and moment of inertia for mass. Torque depends on where and at what angle a force is applied. With no net external torque, angular momentum L = Iω is conserved.

read.title: Turning things
text: A force can make an object spin as well as slide. How strongly it twists depends on torque: the force times its lever arm, the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of the force. That is why a doorknob sits far from the hinges and why a longer wrench loosens a stubborn bolt more easily.

Rotational motion follows the same patterns as linear motion with new symbols. Angular velocity ω plays the role of v, angular acceleration α plays the role of a, and the net torque equals the moment of inertia times α. The moment of inertia depends not only on mass but on where the mass sits. Mass far from the axis is harder to spin, so a hoop has a larger moment of inertia than a solid disk of the same mass and radius. Released together on a ramp, the disk rolls to the bottom first because less of its energy is tied up in spinning.

Angular momentum, L = Iω, is conserved whenever the net external torque is zero. A figure skater who pulls her arms in reduces her moment of inertia, so her spin rate rises. Divers, cats, and collapsing stars use the same principle.
